summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vanuatu, and the sources record no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. The operative risk for a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller comes from official posture rather than from statute.

In November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee to draft a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. The framing attaches suspicion to advocacy and public promotion rather than to private conduct, and a foreign visitor has no standing as a resident to argue the distinction.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local law cannot marry or have a marriage registered in Vanuatu.

There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Narrow exceptions exist in the Teaching Service Act 2013, which covers teaching-service staff, and in section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024, which bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of sexual orientation.

Prosecutorial guidance offers the clearest protection a trans visitor can point to if they are a victim of crime. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, the Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the UN joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.

Partner protection is thinner than the criminal law. A 2016 workshop convened by the VPride Foundation and the Vanuatu Women's Centre established that same-sex partners receive no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes instead.

The social climate is conservative. Gay and lesbian travellers and citizens are advised to avoid public displays of affection, and there is no active gay scene.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 workshop was funded by the Secretariat of the Pacific Community and was the first joint LGBTI human-rights event between the two organisations. USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted case of violence against lesbians and a near-invisible LGBTI presence in the courts, which indicates that the protection machinery on paper is rarely invoked.

The VPride Foundation faced opposition from churches, officials and chiefs at its founding; the 2024 policy direction targets the same organised advocacy.
localsOnly:
The Teaching Service Act 2013 protection is confined to the Vanuatu Teaching Service Commission's own recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff-management decisions; it does not reach private employers or other parts of the public service.

The VPride Foundation advocates LGBTQ rights and freedom of speech, has organised awareness events, and first marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia in Vanuatu in 2016. The 2024 policy direction to ban LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion bears on this resident organising rather than on visitors' private conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
The VPride Foundation's founding year is given as 2009 in one source and 2014 in another; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the drafting committee has produced a policy, what legal form it takes, and how it would be enforced are not sourced.

Whether the Marriage Act amendment affects recognition of an existing marriage or the gender marker on identity documents is not sourced.

No data is available on how often the prosecutorial guidance on sexual-orientation and gender-identity hostility is applied in practice.
